newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Threat to Mobutu rises after Kisangani's fall.
newsitem.headline: Threat to Mobutu rises after Kisangani's fall.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko's prospects of holding onto power in Zaire looked significantly weaker after rebels seized the key city of Kisangani and were welcomed as liberators.
Laurent Kabila's rebels were exultant after their biggest victory yet in their five-month war to oust Mobutu. They were in full control of Kisangani on Sunday evening and the city was calm.
The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) has now overrun about one fifth of Africa's third-largest country.

Kisangani is 1,200 km (750 miles) from Kinshasa, Zaire's capital, and in geographic terms the 32-year-old Mobutu government still has the upper hand. But the future seemed increasingly bleak for the ailing president and his supporters.
The rebels, commanded by Kabila's 25-year-old son Joseph, were warmly greeted by many Kisangani residents when they entered the city.
"Hundreds of people lined the streets welcoming the rebels on Saturday as their liberators. It was very festive," a foreign missionary in Kisangani said.
"Personally I have a certain peace and can't even find the words for it. I feel free now," said Pele Lesondja, 32.

Mobutu, 66, a former soldier with the rank of marshall who took power in a 1965 coup, is weak and far away in France where he has spent most of the past eight months after surgery for prostate cancer.
An aide said in France that there were no definite plans for Mobutu's return to Zaire, despite official assurances in Kinshasa last Friday that he would fly back on Monday.
Mobutu's army has always failed to hold its ground since Kabila launched his rebellion on Zaire's eastern border last October.

Kisangani, the army's eastern headquarters until soldiers fled after a looting spree, was no exception. The government recruited some foreign mercenaries, believed to be mostly Bosnian Serbs, to try to put some backbone into the demoralised troops.
Joseph Kabila, operational commander for the rebels' northern sector, told Reuters in Kisangani he believed most of the mercenaries flew out of the city on Friday night.
Civilian support for his father Laurent is not restricted to areas now controlled by the veteran former Marxist.
"His army is an army of liberation and he must free us of from the dictatorship of Mobutu," opposition militant Jose Wasunde, 34, told Reuters in Kinshasa.
The rebels have not had to fight a serious battle in their offensive and civilians in captured areas frequently voice relief that the wildly indisciplined government troops have left.

The rebels say their next target is Lubumbashi, capital of the mineral-rich Shaba region whose copper, cobalt and precious metals should make Zaire a well-off country instead of one of the poorest in the world.
The capture of Kisangani complicated international mediation efforts. The rebels say they will not agree a ceasefire before negotiations and they insist talks must centre on Mobutu's departure.
It was also another disaster for the 370,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees stranded in eastern Zaire who have trekked ahead of the rebel advance for the past five months.

They are the rump of the Hutus who fled in fear of retaliation for the genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994. Their defeated army has fought with Zaire's troops against Kabila's rebels, who include many ethnic Tutsis.
Kisangani, the most easterly navigable point on the great Zaire river, was immortalised by novelist Joseph Conrad in "Heart of Darkness".
It was also the setting for "A Bend in the River", by the Trinidadian author V.S. Naipaul, who was stunned by the decay and corruption he found there at the height of Mobutu's rule.
